analysis.one_liner: Creates a national handgun licensing and registration system, bans assault weapons and cheap handguns, and raises gun taxes.
analysis.headline: The Gun Violence Prevention Act of 1994 was referred to three House committees, sent to subcommittees, and never received a vote before the 103rd Congress ended in January 1995.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have required every handgun buyer to get a state-issued license and register the gun, imposed a seven-day waiting period, limited purchases to one handgun a month, and banned semiautomatic assault weapons and low-cost 'Saturday night special' handguns. It would have raised dealer fees, required dealer liability insurance, taxed handgun ammunition heavily to fund hospital care for gunshot victims, and capped most people at 20 firearms and 1,000 rounds. It was sent to three House committees and died in subcommittee without ever coming to a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: People exposed to gun violence would gain from licensing, registration, waiting periods, safe-storage rules, childproofing requirements, and bans on assault weapons and large-capacity magazines. Hospitals and trauma centers treating uninsured gunshot victims would gain a new federal grant fund paid for by a tax on handguns and ammunition.
analysis.who_benefits_short: People exposed to gun violence; hospitals

how_it_helps.text: Requires a state handgun license, safety course, photo ID, and a seven-day waiting period before any handgun or handgun ammunition can be transferred, with an expedited process for people under threat of death.

Bans manufacture, transfer, and possession of semiautomatic assault weapons, 'Saturday night special' handguns, large-capacity magazines holding more than 6 rounds, silencers, and certain armor-piercing-style ammunition.

Bars firearm transfers to people convicted of violent crimes or subject to protective orders, sets minimum ages of 21 for handguns and 16 for long guns, and makes it a federal crime to leave a loaded firearm where an unsupervised child can reach it.
Raises the federal handgun tax to 30% and handgun ammunition to 50%, routing the money to a Health Care Trust Fund that pays hospitals and trauma centers for uncompensated care to gunshot victims.

Imposes new rules on gun sellers, including higher license fees ($1,000 per year for dealers, up from $90 per 3 years), liability insurance, more frequent federal inspections, background checks on employees, and 24-hour theft reporting.
Authorizes $200 million in startup grants to states to build licensing and registration systems.

analysis.who_pays: Gun owners would bear new license, registration, safety-course, and arsenal-license fees, a one-handgun-per-month limit, a 20-gun possession cap, and registration of their handguns. Gun manufacturers and dealers would lose the assault weapon, Saturday-night-special, and large-magazine market and pay sharply higher fees and insurance costs.
analysis.who_pays_short: Gun owners and the firearms industry

drawbacks.text: The licensing, registration, safety-course, and fee requirements would fall on lawful buyers rather than on people who obtain guns illegally, and a chief law enforcement officer's decision on a license would hinge partly on fingerprint-based record checks that some states were not equipped to run.

Banning inexpensive 'Saturday night special' handguns and taxing handgun ammunition at 50% would remove the cheapest self-defense options from lower-income buyers, a cost its supporters would have to weigh against the safety rationale.

Capping private possession at 20 firearms and 1,000 rounds of ammunition, with a $300 license and full dealer-style obligations to exceed it, would impose new paperwork and fees on collectors and others who keep multiple guns.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill is a comprehensive, well-developed package: it pairs its restrictions with grants for state systems, targeted money for trauma care, and tax incentives for gun buybacks. But its burdens are broad — licensing, registration, purchase limits, and possession caps touch every lawful gun owner, and its bans on cheap handguns raise a real equity concern for people who relied on those guns for self-defense. Whether the public-safety gains outweighed those costs was never debated on the House floor; the record ends at subcommittee referral.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to three House committees, then to two subcommittees, and no committee ever reported it, so it never came up for a vote and died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Schumer introduced the bill on March 1, 1994, and it was referred to the House Committees on Energy and Commerce, Judiciary, and Ways and Means.
In March 1994 it was referred to the Judiciary Subcommittee on Crime and Criminal Justice and the Energy and Commerce Subcommittee on Health and the Environment.
Additional sponsors were added on October 27, 1994 — Abercrombie, Schroeder, and Kreidler — but no committee action, floor vote, or hearing appears in the record after that.
The bill died in subcommittee when the 103rd Congress ended on January 3, 1995, and all bills not enacted expire.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Firearms manufacturers, dealers, and ammunition sellers avoided new licensing, fees, insurance mandates, inspections, and bans on several product lines; gun owners avoided licensing, registration, purchase limits, and possession caps.

for.name: Chuck Schumer
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and shepherded the text through introduction; no committee or floor action followed.

for.name: Norman Abercrombie, Patricia Schroeder, and Jay Kreidler
for.what_they_did: Signed on as additional sponsors late in the session.

against.name: House Judiciary, Ways and Means, and Energy and Commerce Committees
against.role: Committees to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a markup or reported the bill; it stayed in subcommittee until the Congress ended.

against.name: National Rifle Association
against.what_they_did: Opposed comprehensive federal handgun licensing and registration legislation of the era.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken, so no partisan split appears in the record; the sponsor and all three cosponsors were House Democrats.

industries.note: The bill bans several major product categories — assault weapons, Saturday-night specials, large-capacity magazines — and raises dealer license fees from $90 per three years to $1,000 per year, requires $100,000 liability insurance, and triples inspection frequency. Dealers had a direct financial stake in defeating it.
The bill imposes dealer licensing and recordkeeping on ammunition and taxes handgun ammunition at 50% to fund trauma care, directly raising the price of the product.
A new Health Care Trust Fund, paid for by handgun and ammunition taxes, would reimburse hospitals with substantial uncompensated costs from treating gunshot victims.
Every gun dealer would have to certify coverage of a personal-injury policy with $100,000 limits, creating a new mandated market for insurers.
